newsitem.title: FRANCE: ATHLEICS-DEVERS WINS IN DRAMATIC FASHION, AGAIN.
newsitem.headline: ATHLEICS-DEVERS WINS IN DRAMATIC FASHION, AGAIN.

text.p: Gail Devers had to overcome an unusual gun, a controversial finish and a painful calf to take gold over 60 metres in the indoor world championships on Friday.
But the Olympic 100 metres champion rarely wins the easy way.
The American, who won in Atlanta by five-thousandths of a second ahead of Merlene Ottey, started her day with complaints about both the starter and the gun.
"He's a very quick starter," she said. "There's hardly time to get set. The gun is odd, it doesn't sound like a gun."
Then, at the end of her semifinal, she felt pain in her calf and slowed down slightly, apparently finishing behind Greek Ekaterini Thanou.

The race was won by Russian Irina Privalova and with only two from each semifinal qualifying for the final, Devers survived a scare when she was given the same time of 7.15 as Thanou as they finished equal second.
The times were then taken to thousandths of a second and Devers was awarded second place while Thanou was eliminated. The decision was upheld despite an official protest by the Greek Federation.
"Everyone was telling me that I was clearly second, even Irina told me that, and I didn't know what was going on," Devers said.

In the final, world record holder Privalova made the strongest start but soon dropped back because of a pulled thigh muscle and Devers won ahead of Chandra Sturrup of the Bahamas and Frederique Bangue of France, second and third respectively.

"After crossing the line, I turned back and couldn't see Irina," Devers said. "I understood what had happened and I felt sorry for her. My heart dropped. Irina is somebody I respect very much and you can't rejoice when somebody gets hurts."
Shortly after the race, Devers went to comfort Privalova, who was in tears.
Even before the Atlanta final, Devers had experienced dramatic finishes. In the final of the 1993 world championships in Stuttgart, she beat Ottey by only a few hundredths of a second.
When she heard that her Jamaican rival, suffering from a painful back, would not be in Paris, she might have thought she would enjoy a straightforward victory at last. But it was not to be.
Devers, whose career has been often hampered by injury, has nevertheless built a brilliant record with two Olympic golds, two world titles and one indoor world title before Friday's.
"My life is like a dream, it's full of dreams which come true," she said.
Now 30, she said she would make a new start by cutting her trademark, long fingernails, which were painted in a lurid, blue colour on Friday.
"I'm about to cut them," she said. "I've had them for a long time, it's time to start over."
